(CNN) -- A crew member on a U.S.-flagged cargo ship captured by pirates off the coast of Somalia is suing his employers, claiming they sent him into pirate-infested waters without adequate protection, his attorney said Monday. Abduwali Abdukhadir Muse has been charged with piracy in federal court in New York. Richard Hicks of Royal Palm Beach, Florida, a crew member on the Maersk Alabama, filed suit Monday against Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited, according to the attorney, Terry Bryant. A spokeswoman for Mobile, Alabama-based Waterman Steamship Corp. said she did not know about the suit and did not immediately comment. A spokeswoman for Maersk Line Limited did not immediately return a call from CNN seeking comment. The Maersk Alabama was hijacked by pirates April 8. Hicks, working as chief steward and preparing food for other crew members, heard over the loudspeaker that pirates were on board, and he and other crew members gathered in the ship's engine room for nearly 12 hours, according to a news release from Bryant. "The engine room was dark and hot, maybe 130 degrees," Hicks said in the news release. "We were all cramping up with heat stroke symptoms when we were able to take a pirate hostage and tried to negotiate the return of our captain." The pirates promised to exchange Capt. Richard Phillips for the pirate hostage, but reneged on that agreement, the news release. Phillips offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew. He was held on a lifeboat until U.S. Navy snipers on a nearby ship fatally shot three pirates, rescued Phillips and arrested a fourth pirate. The ship's owners -- the two companies -- knowingly exposed their employees to danger and took no steps to provide appropriate security and safety for the crew, Bryant alleges. "Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited chose to rely on the United States military and taxpayers to provide after-the-fact rescue operations," Bryant said in the news release. "This choice caused substantially more cost and risk to human life than what would have been incurred by defendants had they provided appropriate levels of security in the first place." Hicks is seeking at least $75,000, and "reserves the right to amend this pleading for a certain amount in the future, as it is too early to determine the maximum amount of plaintiff's damages," according to the suit. Hicks is still suffering from injuries as a result of the incident and is afraid to return to work, the news release said.

# Crew Member Sues Shipping Companies Over Somali Pirate Hijacking

(CNN) -- A crew member aboard the U.S.-flagged cargo ship seized by Somali pirates has filed a lawsuit against his employers, alleging they dispatched him into pirate-infested waters without adequate protective measures, his attorney announced Monday.

Abduwali Abdukhadir Muse has been charged with piracy in federal court in New York in connection with the hijacking.

Richard Hicks, a Royal Palm Beach, Florida resident and crew member aboard the Maersk Alabama, filed suit Monday against Waterman Steamship Corporation and Maersk Line Limited, according to his attorney, Terry Bryant. A spokeswoman for the Mobile, Alabama-based Waterman Steamship Corporation stated she was unaware of the lawsuit and declined immediate comment. A representative for Maersk Line Limited did not immediately respond to CNN's request for comment.

The Maersk Alabama was hijacked by pirates on April 8. Hicks, who served as chief steward and was preparing meals for the crew at the time, heard an announcement over the loudspeaker alerting the crew that pirates had boarded the vessel. He and his fellow crew members subsequently took refuge in the ship's engine room for nearly 12 hours, according to a news release issued by Bryant.

"The engine room was dark and hot, maybe 130 degrees," Hicks recounted in the release. "We were all cramping up with heat stroke symptoms when we were able to take a pirate hostage and tried to negotiate the return of our captain."

Although the pirates initially agreed to exchange Captain Richard Phillips for their captured comrade, they subsequently reneged on this agreement, according to the release. Phillips then volunteered himself as a hostage to secure his crew's freedom and was subsequently held aboard a lifeboat until U.S. Navy snipers, operating from a nearby vessel, fatally shot three of the pirates, rescued Phillips, and apprehended the fourth pirate.

Bryant alleges that the two shipping companies knowingly exposed their employees to danger while failing to implement adequate security and safety measures for the crew. "Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited chose to rely on the United States military and taxpayers to provide after-the-fact rescue operations," Bryant stated in the release. "This choice caused substantially more cost and risk to human life than what would have been incurred by defendants had they provided appropriate levels of security in the first place."

The lawsuit seeks damages of at least $75,000, with Hicks "reserv[ing] the right to amend this pleading for a certain amount in the future, as it is too early to determine the maximum amount of plaintiff's damages."

According to the news release, Hicks continues to suffer from injuries sustained during the incident and remains apprehensive about returning to work.

Federal prosecutors in New York have brought piracy charges against Abduwali Abdukhadir Muse. "The engine room was dark and hot, maybe 130 degrees," Hicks recounted in the release. "We were all cramping up with heat stroke symptoms when we were able to take a pirate hostage and tried to negotiate the return of our captain."

Despite agreeing to trade Captain Richard Phillips for the captured pirate, the hijackers ultimately broke this promise, per the released statement. Phillips subsequently volunteered himself as a captive to secure his crew's release, ending up confined aboard a lifeboat until Navy marksmen stationed on a nearby vessel eliminated three of the pirates, freed Phillips, and captured the remaining pirate.

Bryant's news release quoted him stating: "Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited chose to rely on the United States military and taxpayers to provide after-the-fact rescue operations. This choice caused substantially more cost and risk to human life than what would have been incurred by defendants had they provided appropriate levels of security in the first place."

The lawsuit demands a minimum of $75,000 in damages, though Hicks maintains the option to revise this figure later, noting it remains premature to establish the full extent of his losses. A crew member from the Maersk Alabama, the U.S.-flagged cargo ship that made international headlines in 2009 after being hijacked by Somali pirates, has filed a lawsuit against the vessel's operators, alleging that the companies failed to protect their employees despite clear warnings about the dangers of the shipping route.

Richard Hicks, who served as chief steward aboard the Maersk Alabama during the harrowing incident, has named Waterman Steamship Corporation and Maersk Line Limited as defendants in the suit. According to court documents, Hicks claims that the companies made a deliberate decision to route the vessel through waters near the Somali coast—a region widely recognized within the maritime industry as one of the most dangerous stretches of ocean due to persistent piracy activity—without implementing adequate security measures to protect the crew.

The lawsuit alleges that Waterman Steamship and Maersk Line Limited were fully aware of the escalating piracy threat in the region but chose to prioritize shipping schedules and costs over crew safety. Hicks' legal team argues that the companies could have taken numerous precautions, including hiring armed security teams, equipping the vessel with non-lethal deterrent technology, or altering the ship's route to avoid the most dangerous waters altogether. Instead, the suit contends, the companies gambled with their employees' lives.

Perhaps most damning is the lawsuit's assertion that the shipping companies had essentially outsourced crew protection to the U.S. military, expecting that naval forces would intervene and rescue the crew if and when an attack occurred, rather than investing in preventative security measures. This reactive approach, the suit argues, reflects a troubling pattern in the maritime shipping industry where profit considerations are allowed to supersede basic safety obligations to employees.

The Maersk Alabama incident became one of the most widely publicized piracy cases in recent history when Somali pirates boarded the vessel in April 2009. The standoff that followed captured global attention, particularly after the ship's captain, Richard Phillips, was taken hostage in a lifeboat. The crisis was ultimately resolved when U.S. Navy SEALs launched a rescue operation, killing three of the four pirates and freeing Captain Phillips. The dramatic events were later dramatized in the 2013 film "Captain Phillips," starring Tom Hanks.

While the military rescue was successful, Hicks' lawsuit suggests that the entire ordeal—including the trauma experienced by crew members during the hijacking—could have been prevented had the shipping companies taken their duty of care more seriously from the outset.

Legal experts suggest this case could have far-reaching implications for the maritime shipping industry, potentially establishing new precedents for corporate liability when vessels are sent into known high-risk waters. If successful, the lawsuit could force shipping companies across the industry to reevaluate their security protocols and risk assessment procedures for routes passing through piracy hotspots, not just off the coast of Somalia but in other dangerous maritime regions around the world.

The case also raises broader questions about the relationship between private shipping enterprises and government military resources, particularly whether companies should be allowed to treat naval intervention as a fallback safety net rather than investing in independent protective measures for their crews.

As the lawsuit proceeds through the legal system, it will likely draw significant attention from maritime labor unions, shipping industry stakeholders, and legal observers who are watching closely to see whether courts will hold shipping companies to a higher standard of care when navigating known danger zones. The outcome could reshape how the industry approaches risk management in an era where piracy remains a persistent threat to international shipping lanes.

A former crew member of the Maersk Alabama, the U.S.-flagged cargo ship that was hijacked by Somali pirates in April 2009, has filed a lawsuit against the vessel's owners, alleging the company knowingly sent the ship into dangerous waters without adequate security measures.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court, claims that Maersk Line Limited and Waterman Steamship Corporation ignored repeated warnings about piracy threats in the Gulf of Aden and off the coast of Somalia, and failed to provide the crew with proper safeguards despite mounting evidence of the region's dangers.
